WASHINGTON (CNN) -- If he knew then what he knows now, he might have made some different decisions before the start of the Iraq war in 2003, the outgoing chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff told reporters Friday. Outgoing Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Peter Pace says he now thinks more troops were needed at the war's start. "One of the mistakes I made in my assumptions going in was that the Iraqi people and the Iraqi Army would welcome liberation, that the Iraqi Army, given the opportunity, would stand together for the Iraqi people and be available to them to help serve the new nation," Gen. Peter Pace said. But "they disintegrated in the face of the coalition's first several weeks of combat, so they weren't here," Pace said. Had he known that would happen, he would have recommended more troops be sent at the outset of the Iraq war, he said. In addition, Pace said, if he had been asked in January 2006 whether the United States should build up its Army and Marine Corps contingents in Iraq, he would have said no, because the plan at the time was to build and equip an Iraqi Army and turn over security duties to it. The force was built and equipped, Pace said, but the February bombing of the Golden Mosque -- one of the holiest Shiite sites -- ignited long-simmering tensions between Sunni and Shiite Muslims, further destabilizing the region and cutting short any plans for U.S. troop reduction. Thousands of people have died in reprisal killings and bombings since the attack. Still, Pace said, "Given what I knew at the time, I'm comfortable with the recommendations that I made." Any errors that were made are to be learned from, he added. Watch how Pace details the mistakes made at Iraq war's start » . And he continued to voice his support for the Iraq invasion. "Twenty-six million Iraqis have the opportunity now," he said. "They are working their way through 3½ decades of being trod upon, held down, no opportunity at all for freedom of expression, for living their lives the way they wanted to, for picking [their] leaders." Pace will retire when his two-year term ends this month. Also Friday, Defense Secretary Robert Gates -- in his first public comments since President Bush announced Thursday night he was accepting the Iraq troop level recommendation of Gen. David Petraeus -- noted all Bush's senior military advisers are in agreement with those recommendations. Gates said he asked Pace and Adm. William Fallon, the head of U.S. Central Command, to begin examining U.S. options in Iraq months ago, knowing that Petraeus -- the top U.S. commander in Iraq -- was doing the same. "I wanted the president this month to have the benefit of more than one senior military voice as he considered the next steps in Iraq," Gates said. "I also did not want Gen. Petraeus hanging out there all by himself. "While the analyses of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, CentCom and Gen. Petraeus varied in emphasis and approach, all of the president's senior military advisers are in full agreement with the recommendations made by Gen. Petraeus," he said. The United States' next steps in Iraq, among other things, "had to avoid even the appearance of American failure," Gates said. "Extremist Islam was dramatically empowered by defeating the Soviet Union in Afghanistan. The first attack against us by the extremists, the World Trade Center in 1993, was launched from Afghanistan just four years after the last Soviet soldier left there. "Should the jihadists be able to claim a victory in Iraq over the United States, the sole remaining superpower, I believe it would empower them worldwide far, far more than their victory over the Soviets," Gates said. "The regional consequences would be significant and highly destabilizing." E-mail to a friend .

"One of the mistakes I made in my assumptions going in was that the Iraqi people and the Iraqi Army would welcome liberation, that the Iraqi Army, given the opportunity, would stand together for the Iraqi people and be available to them to help serve the new nation," Gen. Pace explained. Instead, the force "disintegrated in the face of the coalition's first several weeks of combat, so they weren't here." The resulting wave of destabilizing violence and retaliatory killings severely disrupted plans for a U.S. troop reduction. 

Nevertheless, Pace maintained confidence in his past guidance: "Given what I knew at the time, I'm comfortable with the recommendations that I made," adding that any missteps offer valuable lessons for the future.

Despite acknowledging these initial misjudgments, Gen. Pace reaffirmed his support for the decision to invade Iraq. "Twenty-six million Iraqis have the opportunity now," he said. Bush announced Thursday evening that he had accepted the troop-level recommendations of Gen. David Petraeus, the top U.S. commander in Iraq. Petraeus varied in emphasis and approach, all of the president's senior military advisers are in full agreement with the recommendations made by Gen. Petraeus."

Emphasizing the high stakes involved, Gates underscored that future U.S. actions "had to avoid even the appearance of American failure." Drawing a historical comparison, he warned of the dangers of emboldening violent extremists.

**Lessons of Liberation and Strategy: Gen. Peter Pace’s Reflections on the 2003 Iraq War**

As General Peter Pace prepared to conclude his tenure as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, he undertook a candid evaluation of the early strategic decisions that shaped the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Serving as Vice Chairman during the war’s opening phases, Pace was positioned at the highest levels of military decision-making, offering him a unique perspective on the intersection of strategic theory and operational reality. In his final assessments, Pace offered a nuanced reflection on the initial military deployment, examining how pre-war planning assumptions collided with the complex realities on the ground in Baghdad.

At the heart of Pace’s reflection was the debate over troop strength during the initial phase of Operation Iraqi Freedom. War plans had largely relied on a lean, highly mobile force designed to rapidly overwhelm Saddam Hussein’s regular military—a concept heavily influenced by modern doctrines of speed and precision. However, these plans operated under the core assumption that Iraq’s civil infrastructure, police force, and military apparatus would remain largely intact after the regime fell, serving as a stabilizing foundation during the transition to a post-Saddam society. 

Reality quickly proved far more volatile. Following the rapid fall of Baghdad, the expected institutional stability failed to materialize. Instead, the total collapse and institutional dissolution of the Iraqi military created a massive security vacuum across the country. This void was rapidly filled by widespread looting, an emerging insurgency, and brutal sectarian violence. In light of these unforeseen developments, Gen. Pace acknowledged a significant strategic miscalculation: had military planners anticipated the complete disintegration of Iraqi state forces and the swift rise of sectarian warfare, he would have recommended a vastly larger initial U.S. troop deployment. A larger footprint at the outset, he noted, could have secured critical infrastructure, suppressed early civil unrest, and prevented the violent lawlessness that ultimately derailed initial stabilization efforts.

Despite these frank admissions regarding military planning, Pace strongly emphasized that identifying strategic flaws did not equate to condemning the overarching mission. He maintained a steadfast belief in the fundamental justice of the operation, upholding the liberation of the Iraqi people from a brutal dictatorship as a necessary and righteous endeavor. For Pace, recognizing the strategic underestimation of post-invasion dynamics was not a retreat from the cause, but a vital duty of military leadership. 

Ultimately, General Pace’s reflections highlight the essential requirement for armed forces to continuously learn from operational errors without abandoning their core objectives. His assessment stands as a sobering lesson in the limits of military planning, illustrating the profound difficulty of predicting the outcome of conflict and the perpetual need for adaptability, strategic humility, and rigorous self-evaluation in national defense strategy.

For over three decades, the geopolitical fate of Iraq has been inextricably linked to the political corridors of **Washington** and the breaking news studios of **CNN**. This triangular relationship between military policy, broadcast journalism, and Middle Eastern history fundamentally transformed how the world consumes war and diplomacy.

The connection was forged in the early 1990s during the Gulf War, a defining moment that put CNN on the global map. As decisions were made in Washington to launch military operations, CNN became the first network to deliver real-time, 24-hour live coverage from inside Baghdad. For millions of viewers worldwide, the conflict in Iraq was no longer reported after the fact; it was unfolding live on their television screens, soundtracked by sirens and the commentary of journalists broadcasting from hotel rooms.

By 2003, as Washington prepared for the invasion of Iraq, CNN was once again at the forefront of national and international coverage. From the press rooms of the Pentagon and the White House to embedded units alongside troops on the ground, the network provided a continuous feedback loop. Official announcements from Washington officials were instantly broadcast to a global audience, shaping public debate over foreign policy, national security, and the intelligence surrounding weapons of mass destruction.

Throughout the decade that followed, CNN served as a primary lens through which the American public monitored the war's progress, the troop surge, and the eventual drawdown. Updates originating from Washington about diplomatic strategies or military reassignments were immediately paired with field reports from Iraq, illustrating the human and political costs of foreign intervention.

Today, even as Washington’s strategic focus shifts toward other global flashpoints, the region remains a vital subject of political debate and news coverage. The ongoing relationship between the policy decisions crafted in Washington, the journalism produced by networks like CNN, and the evolving reality on the ground in Iraq stands as a landmark era in modern history—one where media and governance became permanently intertwined.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a news report in CNN's style covering outgoing Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Peter Pace admitting mistakes about initial troop levels in Iraq, alongside Defense Secretary Robert Gates' comments supporting Gen. Petraeus.
counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — In a candid assessment as he prepares to step down, outgoing Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Peter Pace acknowledged Thursday that the U.S. military made key miscalculations regarding initial troop levels in Iraq, even as Defense Secretary Robert Gates publicly threw his full weight behind the current strategy led by Gen. David Petraeus.

Pace’s rare admission of past missteps comes at a pivotal moment for the Bush administration, which is facing mounting pressure from a war-weary public and a deeply divided Capitol Hill over the direction of the four-year-old conflict.

Speaking to reporters at the Pentagon, Pace reflected on the early days of the 2003 invasion, conceding that military planners underestimated the complexity of the security vacuum that followed the fall of Saddam Hussein.

"I think that we clearly miscalculated what the environment would be like post-Saddam," Pace said, noting that military leadership initially believed Iraqi civil infrastructure and security forces would remain intact enough to maintain order. "Had we known then what we know now, we certainly would have adjusted our troop footprint accordingly."

Pace’s comments mark a striking departure from the early messaging of the Pentagon under former Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld, which long resisted claims that the initial invasion force was too small to secure the nation against a rising insurgency. 

### Gates Rallies Behind Petraeus

While Pace offered a reflective look at the war's troubled past, current Defense Secretary Robert Gates kept the focus firmly on the present, strongly defending Gen. David Petraeus, the top U.S. commander in Iraq, and the ongoing troop "surge."

With Petraeus scheduled to deliver a high-stakes progress report to Congress next month, Gates urged lawmakers to withhold judgment until the commander presents his on-the-ground assessment.

"Gen. Petraeus has my full confidence, and he has the full support of this department," Gates told reporters alongside Pace. "He is executing a difficult strategy in an extraordinarily complex environment. I believe we must give him the time and the flexibility to see this mission through before drawing sweeping conclusions."

Gates brushed off calls from congressional Democrats for an immediate timeline for troop withdrawals, arguing that any decisions regarding future force reductions should be driven by conditions on the ground in Baghdad, not by political calendars in Washington.

```
[ON-AIR GRAPHIC / LOWER THIRD]
TOPIC: IRAQ AT A CROSSROADS
HEADLINE: PACE ADMITS EARLY TROOP LEVEL ERRORS; GATES BACKS PETRAEUS
```

### Political Tension on the Hill

Pace’s acknowledgment of early errors is likely to fuel arguments from critics who say the Bush administration’s strategy in Iraq has been flawed from the start.

Leading Democrats on Capitol Hill seized on Pace's comments, arguing that the admission underscores the need for a fundamental shift in policy. 

"General Pace’s admission confirms what many of us have been saying for years," said a senior Democratic aide. "The initial planning was disastrously flawed, and doubling down on a surge strategy without a clear exit plan is simply repeating the mistakes of the past."

However, Pentagon officials insist the situation today is vastly different. The surge, which brought roughly 20,000 additional combat troops to Iraq earlier this year, was designed precisely to correct the historical deficit in security forces that Pace highlighted.

### A Transition in Leadership

Pace, the first Marine to serve as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, is set to retire at the end of his term after Gates opted not to re-nominate him for a second two-year stint—a move widely seen as an effort to avoid a contentious Senate confirmation battle over the war's legacy. 

Navy Adm. Mike Mullen has been nominated to succeed Pace as the nation's top military officer.

As Pace prepares to hand over the baton, the military finds itself at a critical juncture: grappling with the lingering consequences of its early missteps while banking heavily on Gen. Petraeus to deliver a breakthrough in a war that continues to define the nation's security landscape.

*CNN's Barbara Starr and Jamie McIntyre contributed to this report.*

counterfactuals.output:
Here is a recreation of a CNN article from March 2007 summarizing Gen. Peter Pace’s statements regarding the misjudgments made during the Iraq War.

***

# Pace: U.S. made 'misjudgments' in Iraq War strategy

**STORY HIGHLIGHTS**
* **Gen. Peter Pace says U.S. leaders underestimated post-invasion sectarian violence**
* **Joint Chiefs chairman points to disbanding Iraqi army as a key miscalculation**
* **Comments come amid intense debate over President Bush's troop "surge"**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The nation’s top military officer acknowledged Tuesday that U.S. military and civilian leaders made critical "misjudgments" during the planning and execution of the Iraq War, particularly regarding the country's post-invasion stability.

Gen. Peter Pace, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, admitted in an interview that key assumptions made prior to the 2003 invasion turned out to be flawed, contributing to the prolonged violence and insurgency currently gripping the nation. 

"If we had known then what we know now, we would have done some things differently," Pace said, offering one of the most candid assessments of the war effort by a high-ranking Pentagon official to date. 

### The Decision to Disband the Army

Among the significant errors highlighted by Pace was the decision made in May 2003 by the Coalition Provisional Authority, led by L. Paul Bremer, to completely disband the Saddam Hussein-era Iraqi military and security services. 

Pace noted that original U.S. war plans assumed the Iraqi army would remain largely intact after the fall of Saddam's regime, allowing Iraqi soldiers to be repurposed for border security and nationwide reconstruction efforts. 

Instead, the decision to dissolve the military left hundreds of thousands of armed, unemployed Iraqis on the streets, many of whom subsequently joined insurgent groups or sectarian militias.

"The assumption was that the Iraqi army would stay together, that we would be able to use them to help secure their own country," Pace said. "When that didn't happen, it created a security vacuum that U.S. forces had to fill."

### Misjudging Sectarian Tension

Pace also acknowledged that American strategists severely underestimated the depth of latent sectarian tensions between Sunni and Shia Iraqis, which exploded into widespread violence following the February 2006 bombing of the Al-Askari mosque in Samarra. 

Planning assumptions had largely relied on the expectation that Iraq’s civilian infrastructure and bureaucratic systems would remain functional after the removal of the Ba'athist regime. When those systems collapsed, U.S. forces were ill-equipped to handle the resulting civil breakdown.

### The Surge Context

Pace’s remarks come at a politically charged moment in Washington. President George W. Bush is currently implementing a "surge" strategy, deploying more than 20,000 additional U.S. combat troops to Iraq in an attempt to stabilize Baghdad and the surrounding regions. 

The strategy faces strong opposition from the newly Democratic-controlled Congress, where lawmakers are pushing for legislation that would tie war funding to a timetable for troop withdrawal. 

While acknowledging past miscalculations, Pace defended the current military leadership and insisted that tactics on the ground are constantly evolving based on lessons learned. He cautioned against setting a rigid deadline for a U.S. pullout, arguing that a hasty exit would embolden extremists and destabilize the broader Middle East.

"We are constantly reassessing," Pace said. "The enemy gets a vote, and we have to adjust our strategy to meet the reality on the ground today, not the reality we hoped for four years ago."

counterfactuals.prompt: Did General Peter Pace ever admit that the US sent too few troops to Iraq? Provide a detailed news summary of his comments.
counterfactuals.output:
**Yes**, General Peter Pace—who served as Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff during the 2003 invasion of Iraq and later as Chairman from 2005 to 2007—did acknowledge that the United States sent an insufficient number of troops to secure Iraq following the overthrow of Saddam Hussein. 

While in office, Pace publicly supported the military plans put forward by Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld, which emphasized a smaller, faster, "light footprint" force. However, as he prepared to leave office in late 2007 and in post-retirement interviews in 2008, General Pace conceded that the U.S. had made a critical miscalculation regarding troop levels.

Below is a detailed news summary of his comments and admissions.

---

### News Summary: General Peter Pace’s Admissions on Iraq Troop Levels

#### 1. The Flawed Assumption of Iraq’s Post-Invasion Stability
In post-retirement addresses—most notably at the National Press Club and in interviews with news outlets in late 2007 and 2008—General Pace explained *why* the initial troop count was too small. 

Pace stated that the U.S. military’s plan was built on a fundamental, flawed assumption: that the Iraqi army, police force, and government ministries would remain intact after Saddam Hussein was removed, allowing them to maintain order while U.S. forces focused on transition. 

When those institutions completely collapsed (further exacerbated by the U.S. decision to disband the Iraqi military), the small U.S. force on the ground was overwhelmed by the resulting security vacuum, looting, and rising insurgency. Pace acknowledged that because the U.S. did not have enough troops to perform law-enforcement and stability operations, the situation deteriorated rapidly.

#### 2. "If We Had Known..."
Pace admitted that had top military officials anticipated the total collapse of Iraqi civil society and security apparatuses, they would have recommended a much larger U.S. troop presence from the outset. 

In a reflection on the invasion strategy, Pace noted:
* **On Force Size:** He conceded that the number of troops sent was sufficient to *defeat* Saddam Hussein’s conventional military, but was vastly inadequate to *secure* the nation afterward.
* **On Strategic Error:** He admitted that senior leaders, including himself, failed to press for contingency plans that included significantly higher troop levels to hold territory and secure the population.

#### 3. Endorsement of the "Surge" as a Correction (2007)
During testimony before Congress in early 2007 regarding President George W. Bush’s proposed "troop surge" (which added over 20,000 combat troops to Iraq), General Pace effectively admitted that existing troop levels were insufficient to meet strategic goals. 

Pace testified that the U.S. military was operating under a "high level of risk" due to stretched forces and inadequate numbers on the ground to halt the sectarian violence in Baghdad. By backing the surge, Pace publicly aligned with the view that the previous, lower troop numbers had failed to provide security.

#### 4. Taking Personal Responsibility
Unlike some officials who blamed politicians or intelligence agencies, Pace took personal responsibility for the misjudgment. 

As Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs under General Richard Myers from 2001 to 2005, Pace was one of the key military officers responsible for reviewing General Tommy Franks' invasion plan. In post-service interviews, Pace stated that he and the military leadership owed the country their best military advice, and in hindsight, the advice regarding post-invasion troop requirements was flawed. He expressed regret over the military's slowness in adapting from a conventional war mindset to a counterinsurgency framework requiring more boots on the ground.

---

### Contextual Impact of His Statements
General Pace’s admissions were significant because he was the highest-ranking uniformed officer in the U.S. military during the height of the Iraq War. His comments confirmed what critics—such as former Army Chief of Staff General Eric Shinseki, who had been sidelined in 2003 for suggesting several hundred thousand troops would be needed—had argued prior to the invasion. Pace's retrospective analysis highlighted a key lesson of the Iraq War: planning for the "phase four" (post-conflict stability) operation requires force levels dictated by the size of the population to be secured, not just the enemy force to be defeated.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** -- As Washington prepares for a defining month of debate over the future of the Iraq War, top Pentagon officials and outgoing military leaders are offering candid reflections on the strategic missteps that derailed the early conflict -- while issuing stark warnings about the risks of a hasty American departure.

With Gen. David Petraeus and Ambassador Ryan Crocker scheduled to deliver their crucial progress report to Congress next week, the military’s top brass is looking back at the crucial turning points that reshaped the war, from the fall of Baghdad to the implementation of President Bush’s "surge" strategy.

### The Disintegration of the Iraqi Army

Reflecting on the early choices that hindered U.S. efforts, outgoing Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Peter Pace pointed to the decision to allow -- and subsequently formalize -- the total dissolution of the Iraqi military in 2003 as a fundamental miscalculation.

Pace, who is set to step down at the end of the month, noted that military planners failed to foresee the complete collapse of Iraq's state infrastructure. The sudden disintegration of the 400,000-strong Iraqi Army left a massive security vacuum that U.S. forces were ill-equipped to fill.

"We clearly did not anticipate the complete breakdown of the Iraqi army and police," Pace remarked in recent discussions regarding the war’s trajectory. 

According to Pace and other senior commanders, the collapse of the military not only left hundreds of thousands of armed, unemployed young men on the streets, but it also forced Coalition forces to rebuild Iraq’s security apparatus entirely from scratch -- a process that delayed stability by years and created an opening for a bloody insurgency to take root.

### The Catalyst: Samarra's Golden Mosque

While the initial post-invasion strategy struggled with the security void, military leaders widely agree that the nature of the conflict changed fundamentally in February 2006. 

The turning point came with the destruction of the Al-Askari Mosque in Samarra, also known as the Golden Mosque. The bombing of one of Shia Islam's holiest sites, orchestrated by Al Qaeda in Iraq, detonated a latent powder keg of sectarian hatred. 

Military strategists now reflect on the Samarra attack as the moment the conflict pivoted from a nationalist insurgency against U.S. forces into a brutal, retaliatory civil war between Sunni and Shia militias. 

The resulting wave of sectarian death-squad violence exposed the flaws in the Pentagon's pre-2007 strategy of consolidating U.S. forces onto large bases and handing off responsibility to ill-prepared Iraqi troops. It was the chaos unleashed by the Golden Mosque bombing that ultimately forced the Bush administration to pivot to the current surge, placing U.S. troops directly into Baghdad neighborhoods to protect civilians.

### Gates Warns Against "Chaos" and Jihadists

As Congress debates whether to begin cutting funding or mandating troop withdrawals, Defense Secretary Robert Gates issued a stern warning about the dangers of pulling back too quickly. 

Addressing the political divide in Washington, Gates cautioned that a rapid withdrawal driven by domestic political frustration would undo the fragile security gains made during the recent surge and hand a historic victory to radical extremists.

Leaving Iraq before the government in Baghdad can stand on its own, Gates warned, would leave the country open to being overrun by jihadists who view the war as a central front in their global campaign against the West.

"A premature withdrawal would leave Iraq in chaos and create a vacuum that would be filled by jihadists," Gates warned, stressing that a sudden retreat would not end the war, but merely transfer it to a more dangerous phase that could destabilize the entire Middle East.

Gates argued that abandoning the effort now would allow groups like Al Qaeda in Iraq to establish a safe haven from which to plan future attacks against the United States and its allies.

### A Critical Moment

The reflections from Pace, Gates, and other senior officers come at what many consider the most crucial political juncture of the war since it began four years ago. 

While top leaders now openly acknowledge the strategic errors of the past -- from the disbanding of the Iraqi forces to the failure to contain sectarian violence after Samarra -- the message from the Pentagon remains firm: whatever mistakes were made in 2003 and 2006, a hasty exit in 2007 could prove far more catastrophic.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you provide the text of the CNN report where Defense Secretary Robert Gates explains why he didn't want Gen. Petraeus "hanging out there all by himself" regarding Iraq troop recommendations?
counterfactuals.output:
The statement you are referring to comes from a Pentagon press briefing on **August 31, 2007**, led by Defense Secretary Robert Gates and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Peter Pace. 

At the time, Washington was preparing for the crucial September 2007 report to Congress regarding the Iraq War "surge," which was to be delivered by Gen. David Petraeus and Ambassador Ryan Crocker. Concerns had been raised that the Bush administration was putting all the responsibility on Petraeus, effectively making him the sole face of the Iraq strategy.

Below is the relevant transcript excerpt from Defense Secretary Robert Gates’ remarks, as reported and broadcast by CNN (with CNN Pentagon Correspondent Jamie McIntyre and anchors reporting on the briefing):

---

### Excerpt from the Pentagon Press Briefing (August 31, 2007)

**DEFENSE SECRETARY ROBERT GATES:** 
> "I don't want Dave Petraeus hanging out there all by himself. General Petraeus is the commander on the ground, and obviously his recommendations will carry extraordinary weight. But there is a chain of command. Admiral Fallon is the combatant commander. I am the Secretary of Defense. The Joint Chiefs of Staff have a statutory role to advise the President. 
> 
> My view is that all of us should have our say, and that we should provide our advice to the President, and then the President will make his decisions. But I think it's very important that the military leadership and the civilian leadership in the department be part of this process, and that General Petraeus not be left out there as though this were entirely his decision."

---

### How CNN Reported It (Analysis & Context)

Following the briefing, **CNN Senior Pentagon Correspondent Jamie McIntyre** provided the following context during CNN’s news coverage:

**JAMIE MCINTYRE (CNN Correspondent):**
> "Defense Secretary Robert Gates made it very clear today that while General David Petraeus’s assessment will carry tremendous weight, he will not be the only one making recommendations to President Bush. 
> 
> Gates told reporters at the Pentagon that he wants to make sure Petraeus is not 'hanging out there all by himself' politically or militarily. Gates emphasized that the chain of command—including Central Command chief Admiral William Fallon, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and Gates himself—will all weigh in before President Bush decides on future troop levels in Iraq.
> 
> This comes amid criticism from Congressional Democrats who argued that the White House was using General Petraeus as a shield against political opposition to the war."

---

### Background Context
Gates made these comments specifically to reinforce that troop decisions were a collective responsibility of the entire national security leadership—both civilian and military—and to counter narratives suggesting that the White House was offloading political responsibility for the Iraq strategy onto General Petraeus alone.
